glossary.gloss: Old-fashioned word for 'you' (singular), used here as Augustine addresses God directly throughout. The whole book is a prayer spoken to God as 'Thou.'
Truly; really. An emphatic word, like saying 'truly' or 'indeed.'
To graciously grant or agree to do something, as a favor from someone higher to someone lower.
To where; in what direction. 'Whither do I call Thee?' means 'To where do I call you?'
From where; from what source. 'Whence canst Thou enter into me?' means 'From where can you enter me?'
From there; from that place.
To here; to this place.
Anything. 'Is there aught in me?' means 'Is there anything in me?'
Nothing. 'Even hadst Thou done nought' means 'even if you had done nothing.'
To rest or settle peacefully. Augustine's famous theme: the heart is restless until it can rest ('repose') in God.
Unable to find peace or rest. From the book's most famous line: 'our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.'
Angry; full of anger. 'Art wroth with me' means 'you are angry with me.'
Deep sorrow or misery; a grievous trouble or calamity.
To intoxicate or make drunk. Used figuratively: Augustine asks God to flood and overwhelm his heart with joy.
Wickedness or gross injustice; sinful wrongdoing.
Violations of God's law; sins, offenses against what is right.
In this old sense, to allow or permit. 'Suffer me to speak' means 'allow me to speak,' not 'cause me pain.'
A biblical phrase for human lowliness and mortality — a reminder that a person is frail, humble, and bound to die.
A maker or craftsman. 'Shall any be his own artificer?' asks whether anyone can create himself.
God's wise care and governing of the world and of each life — the belief that God guides everything for good.
One who humbly begs or prays; a petitioner asking earnestly for help.
Reluctant; unwilling. 'I am loth to count it' means 'I am reluctant to count it.'
To beg or implore earnestly. 'I beseech Thee' means 'I beg you.'
A phrase from the Psalms meaning born already tainted by sin — Augustine's idea that sinfulness is present from the very beginning of life.
The Christian doctrine that all humans inherit a fallen, sinful nature from Adam, the first man — a guilt present even before any personal wrongdoing.
A trace or remaining mark of something. 'No vestige' means 'no trace at all.'
Skill in speaking and language — rhetoric and eloquence, the prized education of Augustine's day.
Blows from a whip or rod; a beating. Schoolboys were 'beaten with stripes' as punishment.
Gladly, willingly; or obliged to. 'We were fain to pass' means 'we were obliged (or content) to pass.'
Instruments of torture. Augustine compares the schoolboy's fear of beatings to a martyr's fear of torture racks.
Endowed or supplied with a quality. 'Endued with so great a spirit' means 'given so great a spirit.'
Feels or expresses pity for someone's suffering; sympathizes.
In an unbecoming or improper way; shamefully.
The legendary Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid. As a schoolboy Augustine wept over Aeneas's story while ignoring his own spiritual death.
The queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid who killed herself for love of Aeneas. Augustine wept for her fate as a boy.
Aeneas's wife in Virgil's Aeneid, who died during the fall of Troy; her ghost appears to him. Augustine mentions 'Creusa's shade.'
The ancient city destroyed by the Greeks in the Trojan War, as told in Homer and Virgil. Its burning was a favorite schoolboy tale.
The great Roman poet (70–19 BC), author of the Aeneid, which young Augustine studied and loved.
The legendary ancient Greek poet of the Iliad and Odyssey. Augustine, struggling with Greek, found Homer 'bitter to my boyish taste.'
Jupiter, king of the Roman gods. Augustine scorns the myths of 'Jove the thunderer and the adulterer' as bad moral examples.
Queen of the Roman gods, wife of Jupiter, famous for her rage. Augustine had to compose a speech imitating her anger as a school exercise.
In Greek myth, the woman Jupiter seduced by appearing as a shower of gold. Augustine cites the tale as an immoral myth taught to boys.
A Roman comic playwright (c. 195–159 BC). Augustine criticizes a scene from Terence in which a youth excuses lust by pointing to Jupiter's example.
A grammatical mistake or error in language. Augustine notes people felt more shame over a solecism than over an immoral life.
A mistake in speech — a mispronounced or misused word. Schoolboys feared committing a 'barbarism' more than committing a sin.
Hidden, obscure, or hard to understand. 'Aught recondite' means 'anything deep or mysterious.'
The great city in North Africa (near modern Tunis) where Augustine went to study rhetoric. He calls it 'a cauldron of unholy loves.'
Augustine's hometown in Roman North Africa (modern Souk Ahras, Algeria), where his father Patricius was a poor freeman.
A nearby North African town where the young Augustine was first sent to study grammar and rhetoric.
Strong, disordered desire, especially sexual lust or craving for physical pleasure — a central word for the appetites Augustine struggled with.
In Christian usage, human nature in its weak, sinful, bodily appetites — opposed to the spirit. Not just the body, but the pull toward sin.
Sexual sin outside marriage. Augustine also uses it figuratively: turning away from God to love lesser things is 'fornication against Thee.'
Shameful wickedness; scandalous, disgraceful vice. The young Augustine even boasted of vices he hadn't committed.
Intense, ungoverned desire — usually sexual craving, but also any greedy appetite that overrules reason.
Sexually pure; refraining from forbidden desire. Augustine's mother urged him to be 'chaste.'
In the early church, a person being instructed in the faith and preparing for baptism, but not yet baptized. Augustine's father was one 'but recently.'
The Christian rite of washing with water that marks entry into the faith and the cleansing of sins. Augustine's baptism was deferred in his youth.

Augustine's devout Christian mother, who wept and prayed for his conversion for years. He calls her 'Thy faithful one' and 'Thy handmaid.' (Pusey does not name her in these books, but she is the mother throughout.)
Augustine's father, a 'poor freeman of Thagaste,' not yet a Christian during Augustine's youth and chiefly concerned with his son's career. (Pusey calls him only 'my father.')
A female servant. Augustine repeatedly calls himself 'the son of Thy handmaid,' meaning the son of God's faithful servant (his mother).
The wicked ancient city, used here as a symbol of a sinful, godless world. Augustine 'walked the streets of Babylon' as an image of his immoral life.
A Roman noble (c. 108–62 BC) infamous for his conspiracy against Rome. Augustine cites him as an example of someone who did evil for the sake of some further gain.
God's free, unearned favor and help, which forgives sin and enables a person to do good. 'To Thy grace I ascribe it' — Augustine credits all his good to grace.
God's compassion and willingness to forgive rather than punish. A constant theme: Augustine appeals to God's mercy throughout.
The inner, spiritual self — the seat of mind, will, and love, made for God. Augustine speaks to and about his own soul constantly.
To give back to God; to repay or offer to him. A biblical phrase ('What shall I render unto the Lord?').
One who lures or entices deceitfully. Augustine calls bad friendship an 'inveigler of the soul.'
Reckless, undisciplined indulgence, often sexual; playful mischief without restraint.
Pleasing in appearance; attractive, beautiful, fitting.
Empty, unproductive, fruitless. 'I became to myself a barren land' means his soul felt desolate.
Followers of Manichaeism, a religion Augustine belonged to for about nine years. They taught that two eternal powers, good (light) and evil (darkness), are at war, and that God has a bodily nature.
Mani (c. 216–274), the Persian founder of the Manichaean religion. Augustine criticizes his many writings about the heavens and stars as false.
Among the Manichees, the inner circle of strict, holy members, served by ordinary followers ('Hearers'). Augustine mocks their claim to release divine 'particles' from food.
The great Roman orator and philosopher (106–43 BC). His lost work Hortensius, which Augustine read at nineteen, turned his heart toward the love of wisdom.
A now-lost dialogue by Cicero urging the pursuit of philosophy. Reading it was a turning point that awakened Augustine's longing for wisdom and God.
Literally 'love of wisdom.' Augustine came to long for true wisdom, but warns against false philosophy that leads away from Christ.
In Christian theology, the eternal Son of God, Christ, through whom all things were made (from the Gospel of John). Augustine says the proud philosophers 'knew not the way, Thy Word.'
A title for the Holy Spirit, meaning Comforter or Helper. Augustine lists it among the names the Manichees mouthed without true faith.
The divine nature; God considered as the supreme being. 'In Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.'
Jesus, the Son of God and savior. Augustine says Christ's name, drunk in with his mother's milk, kept its hold even in his years of error.
The Christian belief that God's Son became a human being, born of the Virgin Mary. Augustine refers to faith 'through the Incarnation of Thy Son.'
The mother of Jesus, who conceived him while remaining a virgin. Augustine's Manichaean error made him unable to believe Christ was truly born of her.
The sacred writings of the Bible — the Old Testament (Law and Prophets) and New Testament. Augustine first found Scripture too plain and lowly for his proud taste.
The ten core laws God gave Moses. Augustine calls them 'that psaltery of ten strings,' the standard against which sin is measured.
The patriarch and father of the people of Israel, counted righteous in the Bible. Augustine lists him among the holy men he had wrongly judged.
Son of Abraham, one of the Hebrew patriarchs counted righteous in Scripture.
Son of Isaac, a Hebrew patriarch whose twelve sons fathered the tribes of Israel.
The great prophet who led Israel out of Egypt and received God's law. Augustine names him among the righteous he once judged unfairly.
The shepherd who became king of Israel and is traditionally the author of many Psalms. Augustine counts him among the righteous of old.
The biblical city destroyed for its wickedness. Augustine refers to 'the men of Sodom' as an example of offenses against nature.
The first man in the Bible, whose sin (the Fall) brought sin and death to all humanity. 'The sons of Adam' means all people; 'we all die in Adam.'
The first woman in the Bible. 'The sons of Eve' means humankind; 'the inheritance of Eve' refers to a mother's pain in bringing forth children.
Utter ruin; eternal damnation, the loss of the soul. Augustine's mother wept for his feared 'perdition.'
A belief that contradicts the official teaching of the church. Augustine's Manichaeism was such a heresy.
Lack of reverence for God; ungodliness, irreligion.
Devout reverence and faithful service toward God; true religious devotion. Augustine contrasts genuine piety with empty knowledge.
Showing gross disrespect for sacred or holy things; profaning what is divine.
An old word for 'various' or 'several.' 'Divers lusts' means 'various lusts.'
Chattering or talking foolishly and emptily. 'Men proudly doting, exceeding carnal and prating.'
An archaic word for lying or falsehood. 'Such as loved vanity, and sought after leasing.'
A close friend of Augustine, 'a youth singularly good,' who mocked astrology and divination.
Here it means astrologers — those who claimed to read fate in the stars, not mathematicians in the modern sense. Augustine consulted them.
The attempt to foretell the future or learn hidden things by signs, stars, or magic. Augustine eventually rejected it.
The Roman goddess of love, also the planet. Astrologers blamed sins on planetary influences: 'This did Venus, or Saturn, or Mars.'
A Roman god and a planet, invoked by astrologers as a cause of human fate.
The Roman god of war and a planet, named by astrologers as shaping people's actions and sins.
The art of medicine; healing. 'A wise man, very skilful in physic' means skilled in medicine.
The ancient Greek 'father of medicine.' The wise old physician who advised Augustine had studied works like those of Hippocrates.
Belonging to a proconsul, a high Roman provincial governor. The man placed a garland on Augustine 'with his own proconsular hand.'
A prize wreath awarded for winning a public contest of poetry or oratory. Augustine won such a crown.
In Greek legend, two devoted friends so loyal that each was ready to die for the other. Augustine recalls them while grieving his dead friend.
Eased, soothed, or lessened. 'Time hath assuaged my wound' means time had softened his grief.
A figment of the imagination; an unreal mental image. Augustine had imagined God as a mere 'phantasm,' a false picture.
Bodily; having physical form and substance. Augustine's error was imagining God as something corporeal.
Without a body; immaterial, spiritual. Augustine could not yet conceive of God as an incorporeal substance.
A philosophical term for a single, indivisible unit or oneness. Augustine wrongly imagined the rational soul as a sexless 'Monad.'
A philosophical term for a twofold or divided thing. Augustine wrongly pictured the source of evil and lust as a 'Duad.'
The ten 'categories' in Aristotle's logic (substance, quality, quantity, and so on) used to classify everything. Augustine read this work easily, unaided.
The great ancient Greek philosopher (384–322 BC). Augustine read his treatise on the ten categories ('Predicaments') by himself as a young man.
A famous orator of Rome whom Augustine admired from afar and dedicated his early book 'On the Fair and Fit' to, though he had never met him.
The title of Augustine's lost early book, exploring beauty: the 'fair' (beautiful in itself) and the 'fit' (beautiful in how it suits something else).
Gray or white hair; old age. 'Even to hoar hairs wilt Thou carry us' means God carries us into old age.
A celebrated bishop of the Manichees, famed for eloquence. Augustine eagerly awaited him for years but found him charming yet ignorant of real learning.
A well-known constellation (Ursa Major). Augustine says a humble believer who doesn't even know the Great Bear is better off than a proud astronomer who ignores God.
The two times each year when the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky. Augustine notes the Manichees couldn't explain them.
The two times each year when day and night are equal in length. Augustine cites them among the astronomical facts the Manichees got wrong.
Here, units of measurement for how much of the sun or moon is covered during an eclipse. Astronomers predicted 'how many digits.'
Followers of a school of Greek philosophy (the New Academy) who taught that nothing can be known for certain and one should doubt everything. Augustine briefly leaned their way.
A high Roman official governing a city. Symmachus, 'prefect of the city,' tested Augustine and sent him to Milan.
The pagan prefect of Rome who, after testing him, appointed Augustine as the official rhetoric teacher for Milan.
The northern Italian city where Augustine went to teach rhetoric and met Bishop Ambrose — a key step toward his conversion.
The revered bishop of Milan, 'among the best of men,' whose preaching and kindness drew Augustine gradually back toward the Christian faith.
The capital of the empire, where Augustine moved to teach rhetoric, hoping for better-behaved students, and where he fell gravely ill.
Belonging to a bishop. Ambrose showed Augustine 'an Episcopal kindness,' a fatherly welcome befitting a bishop.
A famous early Christian bishop and martyr of Carthage. Augustine's mother stayed near a shrine ('Oratory') dedicated to him the night he secretly sailed away.
A small chapel or place set aside for prayer. Augustine left his mother praying at an Oratory honoring Cyprian.
A Christian who debated the Manichees publicly at Carthage, using Scripture against them so effectively that he began to unsettle Augustine's beliefs.
The universal Christian church, holding the orthodox faith — contrasted here with the Manichaean sect. Augustine slowly returned toward it.
Deeply sorry for one's sins; humbly repentant. God does not despise 'a broken and contrite heart.'
An offering made to God, especially in worship or at the altar. Augustine's mother brought the daily 'oblation' to church.
Acts of charity; giving to the poor. Augustine praises his mother as 'frequent in almsdeeds.'
A biblical image for Christ, who is wedded to the human soul or the church. Augustine longs to 'rejoice at the Bridegroom's voice.'
The vault of the heavens; the sky. Used figuratively: the soul 'falling from Thy firmament' means falling from God's heights.
Lending money at interest. Augustine uses it in a paradox about God: 'never covetous, yet exacting usury' — God gives so as to receive back.
Greedily desiring what belongs to others; grasping. 'Covetousness would possess many things.'
Wasteful, reckless extravagance with money or resources. Augustine lists it among vices that imitate God's true generosity.
Laziness; sinful unwillingness to act or work. One of the vices Augustine says pervertedly imitates God's rest.
A rowdy gang of students at Carthage who took pride in bullying and mocking newcomers. 'Subverters' was their boastful nickname.
Persistent, pressing demands; refusing to take no for an answer. The bishop was 'displeased at her importunity.'
A bottomless depth or gulf. Augustine uses it for the unfathomable depth of God's judgments and for the pit of sin.
Being rescued by God from sin and its eternal consequences; the saving of the soul. The deepest thing Augustine's mother prayed for.
The book's central act: openly acknowledging one's sins to God, and also praising and giving thanks to him. The title 'Confessions' means both at once.
Wild, uncontrolled excitement or madness. 'My frenzy' and the students' 'disgraceful frenzy.'
Utterly detestable; deserving to be cursed. 'Execrable iniquity' and 'execrable defilements.'
Things that make one impure or unclean; pollutions of sin. Augustine speaks of being cleansed from his 'defilements.'
The holy men and patriarchs of the Bible (and later, revered early church teachers). Augustine confesses he once 'censured the holy Fathers.'
The Hebrew Scriptures' commandments (the Old Testament Law). The Manichees claimed others tried to graft this Jewish law onto Christianity.
The Christian Scriptures about Jesus and the early church. The Manichees claimed it had been corrupted.
The Hebrew Scriptures (Law and Prophets) shared by Jews and Christians. Hearing them explained 'in a figure' helped persuade Augustine.

Augustine's close friend and former student from his home town, who followed him from Carthage to Rome to Milan. He was cured of his addictions to the circus and gladiator shows, served honestly as a legal assessor, and was baptized alongside Augustine.

Augustine's mother, called throughout 'Thy handmaid.' A devout Christian who followed him over sea and land, wept and prayed for years for his conversion, and died at Ostia soon after seeing him become a Catholic.
Augustine's son, born of his concubine 'after the flesh, of my sin.' Strikingly gifted in mind, he was baptized with his father at Milan and died young.
An aged and holy churchman, spiritual father to Ambrose, whom Augustine visited for counsel. He told Augustine the story of Victorinus's conversion to spur him on.

Marius Victorinus, a celebrated Roman rhetorician and former defender of the pagan gods who converted to Christianity in old age and boldly professed his faith publicly. His story stirred Augustine to imitate him.

A fellow African and high court official who visited Augustine and Alypius, found Paul's epistles on their table, and told the story of two officials at Trier who suddenly abandoned the world to serve God after reading the life of Antony.
A Milanese grammarian and intimate friend who lent Augustine's circle his country house at Cassiacum. Not yet a Christian, he grieved at being left behind, but was baptized before his death.
A young man from Augustine's home city, a former court officer who was baptized before them and joined their devout company. He led the singing of a psalm at Monnica's deathbed.

Antony of Egypt, the famous early Christian monk and hermit. The story of his life, and his own sudden conversion on hearing the Gospel read, became a model that inspired others to renounce the world.

An educated friend who consulted Augustine about astrology. His story of a noble child and a slave born under identical stars yet with opposite fates helped convince Augustine that astrology is empty.
A shrewd old physician who argued against astrology, holding that its successful predictions were merely lucky chance.
A wealthy townsman and lifelong friend of Augustine, the keenest supporter of the friends' scheme to live together in a shared household away from the world.
The mother of the boy-emperor Valentinian, an adherent of the Arian heresy who persecuted Ambrose. Her conflict with the Milan church is the backdrop to the introduction of sung hymns.
The child emperor whose mother Justina, swayed by the Arians, persecuted Ambrose and the Milan church.
The port of Rome where Augustine and his company paused on their way home to Africa, where he and his mother shared their mystical conversation at the window, and where Monnica died.
Verecundus's country estate near Milan where Augustine retired after his conversion to rest, write, and prepare for baptism.
Trier, the imperial city where, as Pontitianus related, two court officials walking in a garden read the life of Antony and abandoned worldly ambition to serve God.
Africa; Augustine's North African homeland, to which his concubine returned and toward which he and his friends were traveling when Monnica died.

Followers of Manichaeism, the dualist sect Augustine had belonged to. They held that good and evil were two opposed substances and that the soul was a fragment of God's own being caught in a struggle with darkness.
The skeptical philosophers of the later Academy, who held that no certain knowledge could be reached. Augustine flirted with their doubt during his crisis.

The Neoplatonic philosophers whose books (in Latin translation) taught Augustine to conceive of God as incorporeal truth. They lifted him toward the immaterial but lacked the humility of Christ incarnate.

Here meaning the universal orthodox Church (the 'Church Catholic') and its faith, as distinct from the Manichees and various heresies. To be a 'Catholic Christian' is what Monnica longed for Augustine to become.

Self-restraint, especially sexual abstinence and mastery of bodily desire. Augustine could not attain it by his own power and personifies it in Book VIII as a chaste, alluring figure beckoning him onward; it is the gift he famously prayed for 'but not yet.'
The woman Augustine had lived with faithfully for years and who bore his son. She was 'torn from his side' to clear the way for a respectable marriage, and returned to Africa.
The faculty of choosing, central to these books: Augustine discovers that his bondage is not two souls warring but a single divided will, half wishing to serve God and half clinging to old habit.
The self's own power to choose, which Augustine comes to see as the source of moral evil ('the cause of our doing ill') rather than any evil substance outside us.
Augustine's turning of will and life to God, culminating in the garden at Milan when, on hearing 'Take up and read,' he opened Paul and all doubt vanished.
Incapable of decay or being damaged; an attribute Augustine was sure must belong to God, since whatever can be corrupted is inferior to what cannot.
Subject to decay or harm. Augustine reasons that the corruptible is always inferior to the incorruptible, so God must be incorruptible.
Augustine's name for God's changeless eternal being, the 'I AM that I AM' that simply *is*, without past or future. He and Monnica strain toward it in the vision at Ostia.
Christ as the one who stands between God and humanity, the 'Man Christ Jesus' whose humble incarnation gives weak souls the strength to reach God.
aliases: that Mediator betwixt God and men

glossary.gloss: The Holy Spirit, the 'Spirit of truth' sent by the risen Christ.
Elders or priests of the church; here, those who offered to let Victorinus make his profession of faith privately.
A high-ranking churchman, here a respectful title for Ambrose the bishop.
A legal officer who advised a judge and helped decide cases. Alypius served as one with notable honesty, refusing bribes and threats.
The Roman arena for chariot races; here the obsessive spectacle that enslaved Alypius until Augustine's chance remark freed him.
The arena where gladiator fights were staged; dragged there against his will, Alypius opened his eyes at the crowd's roar and became addicted to the bloody shows.
A formal speech of lavish praise. Augustine, preparing to deliver one in honor of the Emperor, knew it would be full of flattering lies.
A sticky paste smeared on branches to trap birds; Augustine's image for the clinging pleasure and habit that held his soul fast.
Wealth or money personified as a master, from the Gospel saying about being faithful in 'the unrighteous Mammon.'
A provincial governorship or high official post; the modest worldly station Augustine imagined might satisfy his ambition.
The small garden at the Milan lodging where Augustine, in agony of divided will, heard a child chant 'Take up and read' and was converted on opening Paul.
The chanted words ('Tolle lege') Augustine heard from a neighboring house, which he took as a divine command to open the Scriptures, leading to his conversion.
aliases: Take up and read; Take up and read

glossary.gloss: The tree in the Milan garden under which Augustine cast himself down weeping just before his conversion.
St. Paul, whose epistles Augustine read eagerly after the Platonists and at the moment of his conversion.
The biblical Psalms, which Augustine read with passionate emotion at Cassiacum, especially the fourth Psalm, feeling them kindle his new love of God.
Two martyrs whose long-hidden bodies Ambrose discovered by a vision; their relics, brought to the basilica, were credited with miraculous cures.
Followers of Arianism, the heresy (favored by the empress Justina) that denied the full divinity of Christ.
Followers of Apollinaris, who held that Christ had no human mind or rational soul. Alypius mistakenly thought this was Catholic teaching until he learned otherwise.
A heretic whose error (denying Christ's eternal divinity) is contrasted with the Catholic understanding of 'the Word was made flesh.'
The Greek philosopher who taught that pleasure is the highest good and denied any afterlife. Augustine says Epicurus would have 'won the palm' in his mind but for the soul's immortality.
The biblical twin brothers used as Augustine's proof against astrology: born under the same stars yet with utterly different fates. Esau also figures as the man who sold his birthright.
The Roman emperor who, reviving paganism, forbade Christians to teach rhetoric and the liberal arts; Victorinus gave up his school rather than disobey his faith.
The grape-harvest holiday in the academic calendar; Augustine waited for it to resign his teaching post quietly rather than abruptly.
A hogshead, a large cask or barrel for wine; the vessel young Monnica was sent to draw wine from when she developed a secret taste for it.
A drunkard or habitual wine-drinker; the cutting insult a servant flung at young Monnica that shamed her out of the habit.
Anger or hot temper, in old medicine one of the bodily 'humors.' Patricius was 'fervid in anger,' and Monnica learned never to cross him in it.
In this older sense, a person's whole manner of life and conduct, not just talk. Monnica's 'holy conversation' means her godly way of living.
Aptitude, promise, a natural readiness toward good; Augustine praises Alypius's youthful 'towardliness to virtue.'
Dragged or hauled by force; Alypius was 'haled' into the amphitheatre by his friends against his will.
The frame on which a corpse is carried to burial; Monnica is said to carry Augustine 'upon the bier of her thoughts' as one mourned for dead.
Talked emptily or boastfully; Augustine confesses he had 'prated' confidently about uncertain things he did not understand.
False and malicious accusations; the 'crafty calumnies' the Manichees had raised against the Scriptures.
A quarrelsome, argumentative spirit; Augustine recalls accusing the Church 'with a blind contentiousness.'
Attempts to foretell the future by signs or stars; here the astrologers' practice that Augustine came to reject as empty.
Those who claimed to predict fate from the position of the stars at birth. Augustine abandons belief in their art as mere lucky guessing.
A small round shield; in Augustine's image of proud rebellion, he 'ran against the Lord' with the 'thick bosses of his buckler.'
Augustine's phrase for the soul's estrangement from God, the far country where it is most unlike its Maker.
A scriptural image (from Genesis) for fallen, mortal flesh; Augustine uses it of Christ taking on human weakness.
A scriptural image for the lingering corruption of one's former life that must be purged away.
The 'goodly pearl' of the Gospel parable, the kingdom worth selling everything to buy; Augustine knew he ought to buy it yet hesitated.
The jackal-headed Egyptian god, named in a line of Virgil as one of the 'monster Gods' that the pagan Victorinus had once defended.
The Roman god of the sea, named among the gods of Rome in the Virgil quotation about Victorinus's former idolatry.
The Roman goddess of wisdom, named among Rome's gods in the line on Victorinus's pagan past.
Augustine's term for the pagan idolaters; he calls their gods 'proud daemons' and their devotees 'daemon-worshippers.'
The tall cedars of Lebanon, a scriptural image of proud, lofty things that the Lord brings low; here the haughty pagan nobility and the pride of the Schools.
The rhetorical schools where Augustine taught eloquence; he speaks of their 'lofty cedars' and 'pride' as worldly vanity he was leaving behind.
The classical liberal arts and learned disciplines; Victorinus was master of them, and Julian's law forbade Christians to teach them.
The civic center of Rome, where the eminent Victorinus had been honored with a statue.
A scriptural image of the resting place of the blessed dead; Augustine says his friend Nebridius now 'lives in Abraham's bosom.'
The heavenly Jerusalem, the City of God pictured as a bride; one of the things Augustine found in Scripture but not in the Platonists.
A private religious meeting; here, dismissively, the Manichees' assembly contrasted with the church.
An old small coin; here the lost coin of the Gospel parable that the woman rejoices to find.
A Roman provincial governor; here Sergius Paulus, the proconsul whose conversion is linked to the apostle taking the name Paul.
A sacred Christian rite (chiefly baptism and the Eucharist); to be 'admitted to the first Sacrament' is to become a catechumen.
The Eucharist, the consecrated bread of communion 'rightly celebrated' at the martyrs' shrines.
Archaic verb meaning to refuse or be unwilling, the opposite of 'will.' Augustine: 'I willed, I nilled, I, I myself.'
Greedy or lustful desire; Augustine contrasts giving himself to God's charity rather than 'to mine own cupidity.'
Bondage or slavery; Alypius marveled at Augustine's 'thraldom' to the chain of lust.
To taste, relish, or smell of something; Alypius at first wished their writings to 'savour of the lofty cedars of the Schools.'
Archaic for 'formerly' or 'before'; God converted Monnica's mourning to joy 'in a much more precious way than she erst required.'
Archaic for 'soon' or 'presently'; Augustine's stalling reply to God's call: 'Anon, anon,' 'presently,' which never came to a present.
Accustomed or habitual; 'as she was wont in Afric' means as was her custom. Also 'wonted' for usual.
Archaic past tense of 'dare'; 'who durst intrude on one so intent?'
Archaic past tense of 'forbear,' to refrain or abstain; Monnica 'most willingly forbare' her custom of offerings.
Archaic vocabulary for early or in good time (cf. 'in due season'); the texture of Pusey's diction throughout.
Sparing or moderate, especially in food and drink; Monnica took only 'one small cup of wine, diluted according to her own abstemious habits.'
Temperance and self-restraint, especially in drink; some 'revolt at a lesson of sobriety.'
Persistently demanding; the texture of Monnica's daily, tearful, insistent prayers for her son.
A source of divine truth or a person consulted for it; Augustine calls Ambrose's breast 'that so holy oracle of Thine.'
In old medicine, the turning point of a fever when the patient either recovers or worsens; Monnica saw Augustine's doubt as such a 'sharper fit.'
A faint or loss of consciousness; near her death Monnica 'fell into a swoon' and was briefly withdrawn from her senses.
The shared mystical moment when Augustine and Monnica, leaning at a window, were lifted in thought past all created things to touch eternal Wisdom for one instant.
Augustine's account of his inner conflict: not two souls of two natures (as the Manichees claimed) but one will divided against itself, old habit fighting new resolve.
Augustine's resolved view of evil, learned from the Platonists: evil is not a substance but the corruption or absence of good, 'the perversion of the will turned aside from God.'
The Eucharistic cup of Christ's blood, named among the saving things Augustine found in Scripture but not in the philosophers.
The seasonal school recess (the vintage holiday) Augustine used as cover to retire from teaching.
To that place; to there. People rush 'thither' toward what draws them.
Between. Augustine distinguishes 'betwixt' black and white, or between waking and sleeping.
Why; for what reason. Augustine asks 'wherefore' he recognized truths he had never been taught.
Look; see. A call to pay attention to what follows, as in 'behold, Thou wert within.'
Perhaps; by chance.
At other times. Augustine recalls foul joys with disgust, 'otherwhiles' good ones with longing.
Granted graciously; deigned to give. God has 'vouchsafed' to dwell in Augustine's memory.
Give life to. The soul 'quickenest'—brings to life—the mass of the body.
Too narrow; cramped. The mind is 'too strait to contain itself'—too small to hold all it is.
To cling fast; hold tightly to. Augustine longs to 'cleave' to God and never let go.
To curse; loathe utterly. Recalling shameful past joys, Augustine 'detests and execrates' them.
To try out; put to the test. To 'essay our powers'—to test our strength against temptation.
Approval; praise. The 'approbation of another' increases Augustine's joy more than he wishes.
Votes of approval; expressions of support. Love of praise 'collects men's suffrages'—gathers their applause.
To gently warn or correct. God 'admonishes' Augustine to turn his distracted mind back upward.
Weakened; drained of strength. The soul must not be 'enervated' by the pleasure of music.
Overindulgence, especially in food and drink. The warning not to let hearts be weighed down with 'surfeiting and drunkenness.'
Indulging a desire for pleasure's own sake. Augustine fears disguising sheer 'gratification' under the excuse of bodily need.
Adjusted to the right balance; moderated. The 'bridle of the throat' must be held 'attempered'—kept between too loose and too strict.
Capable of suffering or being changed by feeling. Augustine knows God is 'in no ways passible'—untouched by change or pain.
Empty pride; craving praise for its own sake. Pride can even 'glory in the contempt of vain-glory'—taking pride in seeming humble.
Thinking; the act of gathering scattered ideas in the mind. Augustine notes 'cogitation' comes from a word meaning to collect or re-collect.
Disturbing emotions; passions that trouble the mind. Augustine names four: desire, joy, fear, sorrow.
The vast inner storehouse of images, ideas, feelings, and self-knowledge. This book's central meditation: a 'large and boundless chamber' where Augustine even finds God.
The loss or absence of memory. Augustine puzzles over how he can 'remember forgetfulness' itself.
Living with a sexual partner outside marriage. Augustine notes this is a sin he could cut off entirely, unlike the daily need to eat.
The restless itch to see and know things merely for the experience, even ugly or useless ones. Augustine treats it as a 'disease' and a snare.
True blessedness, which Augustine concludes is nothing but 'joy in the truth'—rejoicing in God, the only lasting happiness.
A trial or enticement to sin. Augustine surveys the daily temptations of taste, smell, hearing, sight, curiosity, and the love of praise.
A testing or ordeal. Augustine asks whether 'the life of man upon earth' is not 'all trial'—one continuous test.
Selfless love—of God and neighbor. It is the love by which Augustine's readers believe his confession and pray for him.
An ancient Greek philosopher who held that air was the divine first principle. Augustine cites him to say the air itself answers, 'Anaximenes was deceived, I am not God.'
Bishop of Alexandria, cited by Augustine for having the psalms read with so little vocal inflection that it was nearer speech than song.
Here the heavenly homeland—'our pure and holy country'—the city of God Augustine longs for, not the earthly town.
Truly; in reality. An emphatic way of saying 'indeed.'
To; toward. An old preposition meaning simply 'to.'
To listen; to pay attention. A plea for God to hear.
A silent signal or command, like a nod or beckon. 'At Thy beck' means at your slightest command.
Dark; shadowy and obscure. Here, the hidden, hard-to-understand passages of Scripture.
Male deer; stags. A poetic image for souls that roam and rest in the depths of Scripture.
To chew over slowly, as cattle do; figuratively, to ponder and meditate deeply.
Clothing, especially fine or showy clothing.
A long journey, especially a sacred one. Here, earthly life seen as a journey toward God.
The one and only Son, uniquely born of God. A title for Christ.
The opening words of Genesis, which Augustine meditates on throughout. The moment, or rather the eternal Word, from which God created heaven and earth.
From here; from this place or life. 'Passed hence' means departed (died).
Immediately; at once.
Equally eternal; existing eternally alongside. The Word is coeternal with God the Father.
Timeless, changeless existence in which nothing passes away and the whole is always present. God's mode of being, opposed to time. This is Augustine's central theme.
The realm of succession, where things come to be and pass away — past, present, and future. Augustine famously asks what it is and concludes he can measure it without being able to define it.
Truth. Here, the eternal Truth which is God.
A title for Christ, whose 'voice' the faithful rejoice to hear; the Church is imagined as his bride.
Yeast that ferments dough; figuratively, a corrupting old influence. 'Old leaven' means stale, mistaken ideas.
Worked; did or made. Old past tense of 'work.' 'Wrought not' means 'did no work.'
Before now; in the past.
The essential being or nature of a thing. God's will belongs to God's very Substance, which is eternal.
Lofty grandeur; supreme height. God precedes all things 'by the sublimity' of his ever-present eternity.
Those who pry; nosy people poking into things that don't concern them. A jesting answer says hell is prepared for 'pryers into mysteries.'
Wandering; rambling off the point. An 'excursive brain' roams idly over imagined past ages.
Already past; gone by. 'Forepassed times' are bygone ages.
To go without; to abstain from. 'Forego working' means to refrain from working.
Now passing; presently running. 'The current month' is the one going on right now.
A drawing-out or stretching in length, here of time. Augustine wonders whether time is a 'protraction' of the mind itself.

The mind's being stretched across past, present, and future as it expects, attends to, and remembers. Augustine's answer to what time is: a stretching-out of the soul. Pusey renders the verb as 'distended.'
Here, not mere inattention but a being pulled apart and scattered across many times and things — the opposite of being collected in God's eternal unity.
Gathered back together into one. Augustine longs to be re-collected from his scattered state and reunited in God.
Many and various; of many kinds. His 'manifold distractions' are his many scattered concerns.
The one-after-another sequence in which temporal things and words occur, unlike God's Word, which is spoken all at once and eternally.
Listen; pay attention. An old imperative: 'list, it ceases' means 'listen, it stops.'
A continuous, unbroken course or flow. A voice sounding 'in one continued tenor' goes on without interruption.
An old unit of length (a few yards). Used as an example of measuring a longer space by a shorter one (a cubit).
An ancient unit of length, roughly the forearm (about 18 inches).
Latin for 'God, Creator of all things' — the opening of a hymn by Ambrose. Augustine uses its alternating short and long syllables as his example for measuring time.
Range of sight or understanding. 'Too far is this way of my ken' means it is beyond my grasp.
To contradict or deny.
Perhaps; maybe.
You (plural), archaic. Used when addressing more than one person.
Often; frequently.
To talk or confer, especially to discuss or negotiate. 'With these I now parley a little.'
One who contradicts or denies; an opponent in argument.
Just begun; not yet developed or formed; in an early, incomplete state.
Fitting; proper; suitable. 'It being meet ever to behold Thy face.'
To grow or become. 'Whence it would wax dark, and chill.'
Change; alternation; the turning of things from one state to another. Augustine ties it to the passing of time.
Unchangeable; not subject to alteration. Said of God's eternal nature.
A small amount or limited measure. 'Out of a narrow scantling of language.'
To compose or write down (a text). 'Were I to indite any thing to have supreme authority.'
Added immediately after; appended. Scripture 'subjoined what earth it spake of.'
To state or declare formally.
A way of naming the Trinity: three Persons that are one God. Augustine pairs it with 'One Trinity.'
To strip bare; to remove the covering of. Augustine must 'uncase' matter of all form to imagine it formless.

The highest, invisible, purely spiritual heaven that belongs to God alone — not the visible sky. Augustine treats it as an intellectual creation that, though created, shares in God's eternity and never changes.

Raw, shapeless 'stuff' that God made first, before giving it any form or beauty — the material out of which the visible world was then shaped. Augustine calls it 'almost nothing,' since it has being but no order or figure.
The Genesis description of the earth before God shaped it: shapeless and empty. Augustine reads it as the formless matter, 'invisible and without form.'
Empty; without content or form. From the Genesis phrase 'without form, and void.'
The Genesis 'deep' over which darkness lay — the dark, unformed abyss before creation took shape. Augustine reads it as a name for formless matter, or for unformed spiritual matter.
For Augustine, simply the absence of light — as silence is the absence of sound. The 'darkness upon the deep' marks formless matter that has no shape to be lit.

Augustine's doctrine that God created the world from no pre-existing material — not out of His own substance and not out of any stuff that already was. Even formless matter was itself made 'out of nothing.'
The capacity to change. Created things are mutable; God is not. Augustine links mutability to time, since change is what time measures.
A purely spiritual, mind-like creation (the heaven of heavens) that contemplates God directly and so escapes the changes of time, though it was still created.
For Augustine, God's eternal Word/Son, the 'Beginning' in whom all things are made — distinguished from a created wisdom (the intellectual creature) that is wise only by contemplating God.
Christ, God's one eternal Son, equal to and of the same substance as the Father — by contrast with creatures, which are made out of nothing.
The Holy Spirit, here the divine author who inspired Moses to write Genesis. Also the Spirit that 'moved upon the waters.'
A high order of angels named in Scripture. Augustine lists them among created things Genesis does not explicitly mention being made.
A name Augustine gives the heaven of heavens — God's spiritual dwelling, the community of holy minds that cleave to Him forever without change.
A scriptural image for God's word or judgment. Augustine wishes God would 'slay' the enemies of truth with it — meaning kill their error, not them.
Belonging to the realm of mind or pure understanding, as opposed to what is grasped by the senses. Augustine pairs 'the intelligible and the sensible.'
Perceivable by the bodily senses; the physical, visible world — as opposed to the intelligible (mental, spiritual) realm.
All-powerful; a title of God. Augustine pairs 'Almighty and Good' to explain why God can make all things good.
Look; behold. An exclamation pointing to something, as in 'and lo, Thy Spirit moved upon the waters.'
Before. 'Ere my life may run into Thy embracements' means before my life may run into your embrace.
A bottomless depth or chasm. Augustine uses it for the downward pull of evil desires and the spiritual fall of angels and human souls.
Formless; shapeless. The 'invisible and without form' state of creation in Genesis before God shapes it — Augustine's image of matter or the soul not yet ordered toward God.

The Christian doctrine that the one God exists as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Augustine finds the Trinity hinted at in the opening of Genesis (God, the Beginning/Word, and the Spirit over the waters).
The first person of the Trinity. In Augustine's reading of Genesis, 'God' who creates heaven and earth corresponds to the Father.
The second person of the Trinity, God's eternal Wisdom and Word. Augustine identifies the 'Beginning' in which God created all things with the Son.

The Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity. 'Ghost' is the old word for 'spirit.' Augustine identifies it with the Spirit borne over the waters in Genesis and with God's gift of love poured into our hearts.
Christ, God's eternal Word; also the gospel message held forth by the saints, shining like lights in the firmament of Scripture.
Carried over the waters — echoing Genesis, 'the Spirit of God moved over the waters.' Augustine takes it to mean the Holy Spirit hovers above all changeable things and lifts the soul upward by love.
In Genesis, the waters God placed above the dome of the sky. Augustine reads them as the immortal, incorruptible beings (the angels) above Scripture, who behold God directly.

The sun, moon, and stars God set in the firmament in Genesis. Augustine reads them allegorically as the spiritual gifts and the holy teachers who shine with the word of life in the firmament of Scripture.

A way of reading in which the literal images stand for deeper spiritual meanings. Augustine reads the six days of creation allegorically — the firmament as Scripture, the lights as spiritual gifts, the beasts as the soul's passions, and so on.
Sacred Christian rites (such as baptism) and the holy mysteries by which believers are initiated and consecrated. Augustine ties them to the 'moving creatures' brought forth from the waters.
Of the flesh; worldly and unspiritual. 'Carnal men' are those still attached to fleshly things, contrasted with the 'spiritual.' Paul could speak to the Corinthians only as carnal, not spiritual.
The highest heaven — the dwelling of God and the angels, above the visible sky. Augustine uses it for the realm of the purest spiritual creation that cleaves unchangeably to God.
The city of God — the community of the angels and saints who rest in God. Augustine contrasts it with the restless 'city' of the worldly.
The rational creature — beings endowed with reason and understanding (angels and humans). Augustine stresses how noble God made it: nothing less than God can give it rest.
As in a dim or imperfect mirror. From Paul (1 Corinthians 13): we see God only obscurely now, not face to face. Augustine says the Trinity appears to him 'in a glass darkly.'
aliases: through the glass of the heavens

glossary.gloss: Surpassingly high; rising far above all else. Augustine uses it for the Spirit borne high above all changeable things, and for the surpassing 'supereminence of Divinity.'
Unbelief; lack of faith. The 'waters bitter with infidelity' are the unbelieving peoples of the world, contrasted with the 'faithful earth.'
An old spelling of 'lantern.' 'His word is a lanthorn unto thy feet' — God's word is a lantern lighting the way.
A down payment or pledge guaranteeing more to come. Augustine says we have received the Spirit as an 'earnest' — a first installment of the light and life to come.

In Genesis the earth brings forth the 'living soul' (living creatures). Augustine reads it allegorically as the believer whose soul has been made truly alive — disciplined and turned toward God — rather than dead in worldly pleasures.
The seventh day, on which God rested. Augustine reads it as the eternal rest and peace believers will find in God — 'the Sabbath of eternal life' that has no evening.

chapters.1: Augustine opens with a prayer — "our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee" — then turns to his own infancy and school days in Roman North Africa. He watches his small self learn to speak, dodge lessons, and weep for Dido while staying dry-eyed about his own soul. Underneath runs the question: whose praise is a boy actually taught to chase?
chapters.2: Augustine is sixteen, idling at home while his father scrapes together money for his schooling in Carthage, and desire arrives before anyone offers to guide it. The whole book circles one small crime — robbing a pear tree for the pleasure of the theft itself — and asks why we sin when there is nothing to gain.
chapters.3: A student in Carthage, Augustine falls in love with love, with the theater's borrowed griefs, and — through a lost book of Cicero — with wisdom itself. Finding Scripture crude beside Cicero, he joins the Manichees instead, while at home his mother weeps, prays, and receives a dream promising that where she stands, he will one day stand too.
chapters.4: Nine years a Manichee, Augustine teaches rhetoric, keeps a mistress, consults astrologers, and writes his first book. Then a friend of his youth dies, and grief tears him open: he learns what it costs to love mortal things as though they could not be lost.
chapters.5: Faustus, the celebrated Manichee bishop, finally arrives in Carthage — and turns out to be a charming man who cannot answer Augustine's questions. Disenchanted, Augustine slips away to Rome, leaving his mother weeping on the shore, and moves on to Milan, where hearing Ambrose preach begins to change what he thinks the faith actually claims.
chapters.6: In Milan, Ambrose's figurative reading of Scripture dissolves Augustine's old objections, and his mother arrives from Africa, certain of his direction before he is. It is a book of friends — Alypius, swept back into blood-sport by the roar of the amphitheater; loyal Nebridius — and of a drunken beggar whose easy cheer shames Augustine's anxious ambition. A marriage is arranged; certainty is not.
chapters.7: The last intellectual barriers fall. The books of the Platonists teach Augustine to conceive of God as immaterial light and of evil not as a substance but as a corruption of good — yet in all those pages he cannot find the one thing he needs: the Word made flesh. He can see the homeland now; he does not yet know the way.
chapters.8: Everything is believed; nothing is done. Stories of converted men — the old orator Victorinus, the desert monk Antony — press on Augustine's divided will until, weeping under a fig tree in a Milan garden, he hears a child chant "Take up and read," opens Paul, and the long struggle ends in a single sentence.
chapters.9: Augustine resigns his professorship, withdraws with his circle to a country house at Cassiacum, and is baptized in Milan alongside his son Adeodatus and Alypius. Then the book becomes his mother's: her hard girlhood, her patient marriage, the vision they share at a window in Ostia — and her death days later, which he must learn to mourn without shame.
chapters.10: The story catches up to the present, and Augustine turns from what he was to what he is. He wanders the "fields and spacious palaces" of memory — how it holds images, skills, happiness, even God — and then takes an unsparing inventory of the temptations that still pull at him, sense by sense, hour by hour.
chapters.11: Asked what God was doing before He made heaven and earth, Augustine takes the question seriously and follows it into the nature of time itself. Past and future exist nowhere but in the mind — memory, attention, expectation — and time may be nothing but the mind's own stretching. It is one of the most original meditations to survive from the ancient world.
chapters.12: Still on the first verse of Genesis, Augustine ponders the "heaven of heavens" and the formless matter from which all things were shaped. When readers quarrel over what Moses meant, he offers a rule of startling generosity: where many meanings are true, why not believe the author saw them all?
chapters.13: The final book reads the week of creation allegorically, as the story of God forming a church — and a soul — out of darkness. The Trinity, the Spirit brooding over the waters, and love as the soul's true weight carry the argument upward, until the Confessions ends where it began: in rest, the Sabbath that has no evening.

define.gloss: In Roman schooling, the teacher of language and literature — the second stage after basic letters, where boys memorized and recited the poets.
The tree Augustine and his gang strip at sixteen — not for the fruit, which they throw to pigs, but for the thrill of the theft itself; it becomes his case study of sin without a motive.
The measuring-rule of faith on which Monnica stands in her dream, where a shining youth tells her that where she is, her son will one day be also.
The poet Horace's phrase for a beloved friend, which Augustine borrows for the dead companion with whom he felt "one soul in two bodies."
A public professor of rhetoric — the paid civic teaching chair Augustine held at Carthage and later pursued in Rome and Milan.
Paul's maxim — the letter kills, the Spirit gives life — which Ambrose used as a rule for reading Scripture figuratively, dissolving objections Augustine had thought fatal.
The question that held Augustine for a decade — where evil comes from if a good God made everything; he comes to see evil not as a thing but as a corruption of what is good.
Not just the virtue but a person in Augustine's vision — a serene, fruitful mother beckoning from the far side of his hesitation, surrounded by those who have already crossed.
Congregational singing after the manner of the Eastern churches, first instituted at Milan while Ambrose's basilica was under siege — a practice that spread through the Western church.
Augustine's image for the vast inner storehouse of images, skills, and feelings — the terrain he searches through in this book, looking for where God resides in it.
His name for curiosity — the appetite for spectacle, novelty, and knowing for its own sake, one of the three great temptations he inventories.
